Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the Technical Education Act be amended to provide that any balance of the ten million dollars appropriated under the act, unexpended on the 31st March, 1934, shall remain available during any one or more of the five succeeding fiscal years, but no portion thereof shall be paid to any province after the 31st day of March, 1939.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Morand in the chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to know just what act is referred to in this resolution. The Technical Education Act was passed in 1919 and was amended in 1929. There was another act, known as the Vocational Education Act, which was passed in 1931, after the present administration came into office. As I understand it, the act of 1931 has never been put into force and I should like to know if it is the act of 1919 that is referred to.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subtopic: BILL TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman is correct in his statement. The Technical Education Act was passed in 1919 and provided for an appropriation of $10,000,000 to be divided among the provinces as indicated in the act. Six of the provinces have spent their appropriations but three have not. In 1929 the act was amended to extend its provisions until the end of the fiscal year, 1934 and this bill contemplates a further extension until 1939 in order that the moneys unexpended by the three provinces may still be available to them. It has no reference to the Vocational Act which was passed in 1931.

subtopic: BILL TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Have any payments been made out of the 1931 Vocational Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subtopic: BILL TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: BILL TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
I rise at this juncture not to object at all to the extension of this bill, because I think I can say for those on this side of the house that we are thoroughly in accord with the minister and the government in extending the Technical Education Act another five years. But in order that the house may understand what progress has been made in the direction of assisting technical eduction I wish for a moment or two to review what has transpired in this house and this parliament with respect to contributing to the progress of technical education. In 1910 a commission was appointed by the government of the day on the recommendation of the then Minister of Labour who is now leader of the opposition. The commission was formally appointed on June 22, 1910 and finally reported on May 31, 1913. The commission recommended at that time that there should be an appropriation of $3,000,000 per year over a period of approximately ten years, or $30,000,000 altogether. Notwithstanding that fact the government of the day took no action on the recommendation of the report until 1919, and instead of accepting the report of the commission, recommending $3,000,000 a year, the government then appropriated $1,000,000 a year, or $10,000,000 for a ten year period. The agreements under these contracts lapsed in 1929, and 1 had the honour as Minister of Labour of that day of introducing a bill to extend the act a further five years so as to enable the provinces that had not earned their portion of the grant to do so. At that time there had been, lapsed and unexpended, a total of $2,602,286.51. There can be no doubt it is a good move. I could not in this corner catch very clearly the remarks of the leader of the opposition; however I would say that it seems to me that especially at this time of unemployment, some more vigorous policy might be expected from the dominion government with regard to vocational work. Very many of our young people are being forced out of public schools at an early age, a gTeat many of them cannot get beyond the public school, some never get even as far as the high school, and when they go out from school they find no opportunity to secure work. There is the hope that within a year or two there may be some little improvement in that situation, but in the meantime what are we to do with all these young people? I should think that the Labour department might very well put forth some effort to provide for them to secure a better education so that when employment does present itself they will be able to take advantage of the opportunity, and be prepared for a higher grade of employment than they can fit themselves for at present. If these young people are allowed to drift out on the streets in all probability they will contract bad habits, some of them will become criminals, in any case their ability to work will steadily deteriorate. It would seem to me that the relief measures that are in vogue to-day might be supplemented or replaced by a grant for vocational work. I have known in my own city of unemployed boys being gathered together in some of the schools and trained in the evenings in manual work, and during the summer time instructed in managing little garden plots and that kind of thing. This was done by school principals who had the welfare of the boys at heart. speechtext: Every reasonable effort is being made to stop the smuggling which undoubtedly has gone on on this coast for a great many years. Perhaps there will always be some smuggling but in recent times more seizures have been made than at any time in the past. Seven seizures have been made in the last few months on that particular coast involving over 500 individuals. Informations have been laid at the city of Quebec in a great many cases, a large number of prosecutions have taken place and many convictions have been obtained. This incident probably involves the largest seizure that the force has been able to make so far. There is no doubt that the ramifications of the smuggling ring are very intricate but it is felt that the backbone of the institution has been broken at last and that it will not be as difficult in the future to control the situation. We are preparing an improved marine service for preventive work. It has been found that the boats previously engaged in the prevention of smuggling have not been large enough or speedy enough to perform satisfactory service. The craft of the bootleggers have been able to out-distance us time and time again but we have under way a program for the construction of a speedier type of vessel. By the opening of spring or at least by midsummer we hope to have boats in these waters which will be quite as speedy as, if not speedier than, the smugglers' craft. In this way it is hoped that we shall be able to control the situation much better in the future than has been the case in the past.
How will these new boats be apportioned between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that the
present program is to use all the new boats on the Atlantic coast.
Is any use made of the aeroplane service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We cooperate with that service and it has been found to be very valuable. An aeroplane flying over smugglers' row seems to have a very excellent effect but the largest benefit is derived from the information which this service transmits as to the location of the various suspected vessels.
Is that a constant service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: For eight months in the year.
Who is in charge of that branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Squadron Leader Higgins of the air force.

I should like to inquire as
to the system of moieties under which officers are rewarded through the payment of a percentage of the value of the seizure. I understand that that system has been changed. What is the present arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The old system of moieties, with respect to anyone effecting a seizure or giving information resulting in a seizure, has been modified to a very large extent. The individual does not now profit as a result of the fine or of the seizure, but the money which formerly went to the individual is now pooled and goes into a trust fund for the benefit of the force.
Including officers of headquarters staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Including all members
of the force; that is under the authority of an act passed last session.

The impression of the
people in my part of the country is that the Way to do away with smuggling is to reduce the duty on liquor, thus making smuggling unprofitable. The United States by the repeal of prohibition have discouraged smuggling, and I would point out to the minister that if smuggling were not profitable it would disappear overnight. I am old enough to remember the time on the Gaspe coast when fishermen would go to St. Pierre-Miquelon and come back with the odd bottle, sometimes a dozen, and no one would bother about it. It was in 1897 under the late William Paterson that steps began to be taken actively against smuggling in the lower St. Lawrence. Now St. Pierre-Miquelon has gone out of business. The distillers and those interested in the trade in Ontario and Quebec have switched off from St. Pierre-Miquelon; they do not go there any more. There would be no smuggling in Gaspe and Bonaventure if it were made unprofitable, so that instead of spending large sums of money to fight smuggling, if the minister would use his influence to have measures adopted to make smuggling unprofitable he would put an end to the practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt that
our high taxes are very conducive to smuggling, and the situation may become aggravated

Mounted Police Act
with the low taxes which the United States government has proposed in connection with liquors. It may be that the result of that legislation will be rather to increase smuggling in Canada than to reduce it. There is no doubt that if the suggestion of my hon. friend from Bonaventure were put into effect a large amount of smuggling in liquor might vanish, but on the other hand a large amount of revenue would vanish likewise from the treasury of the dominion.

Earlier in the discussion the
minister gave the number of members of the mounted police force for last year. How many members of the old provincial police force are included in the numbers he gave?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: About 90 per cent of the former provincial police forces were taken on the strength of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police when the agreements were made with the various provinces.

At the moment I cannot

90 per cent of the provincial forces had been taken on the new force. Are the other ten per cent taken care of largely by pensions?

What proportion of the old
preventive force, when it was under the direction of the Department of National Revenue, was absorbed into the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

About 90 per cent were

ant detective inspectors be appointed to the preventive force while they remain in the mounted police?

Will the non-commissioned officers employed at present in the protective service be entitled to the rank of assistant inspector?

I wish to direct the attention of the minister to the situation in the Rimouski district. In charge of that very large and most important district is a noncommissioned officer who, in the exercise of his duties, has succeeded in winning the respect of the local population to such an extent that II should like to pay him the compliment of acknowledging here that he has done his work in a most excellent manner. Unfor-tortunately he is only a non-commissioned officer and for this reason is rather badly handicapped in dealing with local judges, magistrates, the mayor and other important citizens in the district. The very fact that he has not a commission is, I say, rather a handicap, and I strongly commend to the minister the meritorious service of this man. I think his name is Sergeant Brunet. I have heard from his superior officers, from the officer administering the local land force in Quebec, Captain Gagnon, and others who speak extremely highly of him, and I have letters of commendation on his behalf from the local clergy and from the municipal and judicial authorities. I take this opportunity therefore of bringing his case to the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am very glad indeed
to have my hon. friend's commendation of the work of the force in his district. In regard to Sergeant Brunet, I think my hon. friend is well aware that he has recently been promoted to the rank of sergeant in the force in recognition of the excellent service he has rendered.

Boys not less than fourteen years of age.
Are any boys engaged in the preventive service?

Would the minister kindly explain subsection (2) of section 4? There is an exception made for the Yukon territory in regard to duties under or in connection with any municipal bylaws, unless authorized by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the present time we have authority to execute the local laws in the Yukon, but this is not the case in the other territories of Canada and unless authority is specially granted for that purpose we do not propose to undertake that work. If authorized by the governor in council, we may be enabled to perform that service in other parts of Canada.

Under what conditions would the minister suggest the governor in council could authorize the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to exercise their police power within one of the ordinary municipalities, say in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In any province in which we have taken over the police work, where the province should request us to operate, for instance, in regard to municipal bylaws.
They will be overriding the ordinary city police force of the municipality.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Only on the request of the local government.
Only on the request of the attorney general of the province will they interfere?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That covers offences within the force.
Will the minister inform the committee whether officers of the mounted police force are permitted to apply to persons who are confined in prison, what is commonly known as the third degree?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The third degree is not recognized in any way in any court or under any conditions in Canada, so far as I am aware, but nothing in connection with that matter arises in this bill.

This section defines certain things which it is not considered the duty of members of the force to do and that is the reason I am bringing this up. I know of a case where an officer of the force visited a prison in which there was a prisoner incarcerated for a crime and he put that prisoner through a category of very strict questions and even threats in connection with another crime of which he suspected the prisoner might have some knowledge. That took place lately in the county gaol of the county of Gloucester and it was done by one of the officers of the force. I shall not reveal the name publicly, but if the minister or the commissioner wishes to have it, I am prepared to give it to him at any time. The case is one in which the officer enters a prison cell, with the consent of the sheriff, takes the prisoner to a private room and puts him under a very severe cross examination in connection with another crime with which the prisoner is not charged, but with the intention of obtaining from him evidence against somebody else. This has been done not only on one occasion but on several

Mounted Police Act
and under the protest of the lawyer who in the first instance defended the prisoner when he was accused of a crime not connected with that to which I am now referring. I want to know if that sort of thing is to be tolerated under the jurisdiction, of the mounted police of 'Canada.
Mr. 'GUTHRIE:	I would certainly say
that it is not to be tolerated and1 if my hon. friend will write me a letter making the complaint, I shall have an investigation made into the circumstances. But I may tell the committee I have had many complaints of this nature from many parts of Canada and I have had occasion to read the evidence m very serious cases which have been tried in the criminal courts of the country. I have read the evidence of accused men in regard to the treatment they have been accorded at the hands of the mounted police. One could hardly imagine stories such as have been told in regard to maltreatment, threats, buffeting and assaults which have gone on in the gaol for the purpose of obtaining confessions and the like. But when those matters have been investigated in court during the hearing of a case where judges and juries have passed upon them, they have gone out of their way to commend the officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and to state there was no truth whatever in the charges. I know the charges are commonly made, but I doubt very much if they actually exist except perhaps in extremely isolated cases.

Is there any regulation to prevent members of the force from marrying?
Mr. 'GUTHRIE:	There is a regulation
against marriage until a constable has served six years or a non-commissioned officer five years in the force.

There is another point to
which I wish to direct the attention of the minister with regard to the administration of the law by the mounted .police. Is it not their duty rather to prevent an infraction of the law than to wait until its commission in order to make arrests?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the first principle of police work.

It might be worth while
to look carefully into the method adopted in certain sections of Canada, especially in New Brunswick, in that respect. For instance, let me give a case in point. Here are two. young boys of tender years, say ten or twelve, who at a time when smelt-fishing is prohibited,
start out with what is commonly known as a dip net for catching smelts out of season. A police officer administering provincial laws -in New Brunswick these laws are now administered by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police-sees these boys making for a place where they can use this net, and he waits until they are making use of it; he does not reprimand them or point out that it is a violation of the law, but arrests them and incarcerates them in prison. Is it not rather his duty to prevent them going to the spot with the utensil they have for violation of the law; to warn them rather than wait until they have, perhaps innocently, violated the law and then take them and throw them into gaol with ordinary criminals? Yet that has been done to my personal knowledge. I draw attention to this not in the way of criticism of the minister but in order that the department may become cognizant of these things and bring about a better condition of affairs in having the law respected.

Might I revert to a question asked by an hon. member on the other side regarding the prohibition of marriage on the part of these officers until they have served for six years? To me that is rather an amazing rule. I am wondering whether the thought is that these men shall become accustomed to obedience before they enter the state of matrimony. But I think there should be some explanation, it seems to me an unfair rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The most forcible objection to allowing marriage at will is the cost to the force. As soon as a constable or officer becomes married he is entitled, as a married man, to allowances for his wife, and children as they come. I think in every army there is restraint on marriage for the same reason. Men as a rule join the mounted police at twenty-one or twenty-two years of age, and it is not considered unreasonable that for six years they may not marry without permission, or five years in the case of non-commissioned officers. It used to be twelve years until two or three years ago when we changed it.

In other words the country
refuses to pay a living wage.
We pay good wages.
It really comes to that, because it seems to me that when a man has attained the age of maturity, twenty-one, he has the right, if he so desires, to take on the duties of citizenship-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, he knows that
regulation when he enlists of course.
Mounted Police Act
-especially in the province of Quebec. It seems to me there is an injustice there, I do not see why these men should not have the same rights and privileges as other citizens.

I would point out that there are many who are already married. I know one instance of a lady who was superintendent of a hospital, she left her position and was married to a police officer last year, and two weeks after the marriage he was dismissed from the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That would be for marrying without permission. If they defy the regulations in that way I think we have to discipline them.

I understand that as the
regulations are no married man will be taken on, and any man who gets married without permission-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Within six years.
-will be dismissed. I am told by the officials that a primary reason for that is that a force composed of single men is more mobile.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, that is one important reason.

That reason would apply
more in the old days when the work of the mounted police was chiefly in the wilder parts of the country and a man might be ordered to go a thousand miles into the wilderness; he of course could not take his wife and family with him. But now the work of the force is changing, much of it is done in the cities, and it seems to me it would be the part of wisdom to take married men on the force or allow them to get married when they like, for a married man will be found more reliable than a single man.

May I ask
if it is still the custom in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon for trials to be taken before deputy superintendents?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the officers of the police are by statute justices of the peace. In remote parts where no other officials are available to take informations and the like, they do act, but it is only in isolated oases. Wherever possible the ordinary authorities are applied to for all judicial proceedings.

I think it is a practice that should be stopped everywhere. In the earlier days, even in the provinces, we had serious complaint about this practice. It does seem unfair that the man who arrests

should also try the person he has arrested. It is an objection I have taken before. I assume it is *ot being done now within any of the provinces, where magistrates are available. But it seems to me that at least in cases where arrest is necessary the prisoner should be kept until some independent party can try him, rather than that the individual who makes the arrest, "runs him down" as we frequently call it in the Northwest Territories, should also try him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The grievance is not a
very marked one, because in the last two and a half years there has only been one case where the officer making the arrest has tried a charge, and that was away up in Great Bear lake district.

But Great
Bear lake is becoming a very important centre.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is now, but it was not so until recently.

Section agreed to.
Section 7 agreed to.

This may
not be the place to ask, but there are one or two cases of men who retired from the mounted police in the city of Edmonton, and have since joined the civil service. They are making application that the time served in the police force, for which they received no pension, might be added to their time of service for superannuation purposes in the civil service.

The other question raised by my hon. friend from West Edmonton is now under consideration; we have had it up on one or two occasions. I do not think there are very many involved.
I think about a half dozen now.

speechtext:
There are a few, and recently a long report was made by the commissioner in regard to that question, but as yet I cannot say what action if any will be taken.

Does the word " officer " mean any man in the ranks or just those of higher ranks?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the Pension Act the distinction is maintained between officers and other ranks, and the object of these amendments, in order to bring them into conformity with the present provisions of the Pension Act, is to carry out those distinctions as between the two.
The point I wanted to make was this: If a man in the ranks is killed, irrespective of whether or not he may be only a beginner, will the widow and children be looked after?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, they will be looked after under this bill, but they were not looked after heretofore. Up to the present when a man was killed in the performance of his duty it was necessary to come to parliament and have a special vote included in the estimates; every year there were votes of that kind in the estimates. In order to avoid that necessity and to make the procedure definite and permanent these sections have been prepared, so that the widow and children of any man who loses his life in the performance of his duty will be pensioned.
In introducing the resolution I think the minister made some reference to twenty years service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not in the case of a man killed.
Has the minister made an estimate of what one-half the retiring allowance would amount to, on the average?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; my hon. friend asked that question previously, and I have figures here. I find that in the case of a man with the rank of corporal the widow would receive about $765 per annum, and in addition there would be $60 for each child.
Up to the age of sixteen?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Sixteen in the ease of a girl and eighteen in the case of a boy.

What
would be the figure in the case of an ordinary constable?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Between $600 and S650.

I only want to point out to the minister that under the workmen's compensation acts in the different provinces the widows of men killed receive about $40 a month and there is an allowance of $10 a month for each child up to sixteen years of age. Surely if a constable is killed while performing his duties for the state his dependents should receive as much consideration as is shown the dependents of those killed in industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think we give a little more consideration.
Not according to these figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it will be a little more than $480 a year for the widow, but it will be $5 a month instead of $10 for the children.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 11, 12 and 13 agreed to.

speechtext:

Mr. V.ALLANCE: Will this legislation be retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, because all the widows who have lost their husbands by reason of service already have been pensioned by means of annual grants made by this parliament. This measure will only take effect when the bill is passed.
The minister mentioned the figure of $760. Is that the retiring allowance of the corporal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Morand in the chair.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I am a little curious myself to know why they make it 999 years in these times. I said to my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) when the bill was up before that I thought it was long enough. I will read the memo to the committee giving the details briefly:
This agreement, dated the 1st May, 1912, provides for the joint use of tracks together with the passenger station and passenger facilities of the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway, and lands occupied thereby at Belleville, Ontario.
In addition, the Canadian Northern Ontario Railway agreed to sell to the Campbellford, Lake Ontario and Western Railway Company certain lands together with lines of railway and telegraph lines constructed thereon.
The lines of railway involved are the old Canadian Northern main line through Belleville and the main line of the Canadian Pacific between Montreal and Toronto.
The term of the agreement is for a period of twenty years from the 1st June, 1914, and, if ratified and confirmed by parliament, is to be effective for nine hundred and ninety-nine (999) years from the 1st June, 1914.
If the committee wants any particular details I shall be glad to give them on the third reading.

answer definitely at the moment, but nearly all the railways in that section of the country which used to be independent are now subsidiaries of either the Canadian Northern, now a part of the Canadian National, or the Canadian Pacific. There are probably no independent railways in that section of the country at the present time.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Are these railways subsidiaries of the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
The Canadian Northern
is now a part of the Canadian National. I cannot answer offhand as to the other railway mentioned in the 'bill, but I can look it up for my hon. friend. I do not know, however, that it really matters, because it is an agreement made by the two railway companies and has been in effect since 1914.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 999 years is
an awfully long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I do not know that my
hon. friend or I need worry about the end of that period.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Would the minister in his
own business recommend a lease of 999 years? Does he not think it is ridiculous on the face of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Not necessarily, because
it is satisfactory to both railways. They are fixing it practically for all time, making a permanent arrangement.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I would suggest that the term be cut down to a reasonable length. It is ridiculous to make it for 999 years. As a business man you would not do it in your own business.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I think that is a fairly
reasonable attitude, and if the committee wishes to cut it down to 99 years I have no objection. One term is about as certain for this committee as the other.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
But 99 years is not quite
so ridiculous as 999 years, in the eyes of the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wants
to make a motion to change it to 99 years-

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I move, Mr. Chairman, that the term be changed to 99 years from 999 years.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Schedule agreed to.
Mr. 'GUTHRIE:	I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that this is an agreement signed by the various parties interested, and if we vary the agreement that they have signed we may find ourselves in trouble. The term of 999 years is not uncommon particularly in English conveyancing where the titles to English property are often on a 999 year lease. The object of that is to prevent an absolute sale and transfer and to retain the control which the landlord has over the tenant. That is no doubt the object in making this particular lease for 999 years. I do not think we should change it. We might hold up the bill and see if the parties would agree to the change, but to change a signed agreement renders the whole thing nugatory.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: It does look ridiculous to make it 999 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: It is a perpetual agreement.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
That is
quite true, but I see from a cursory glance at the bill that the sum involved is not very large and 99 years would seem to be a reasonable term for an agreement of that kind to run.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I think the bill had better stand in committee to see if the companies will agree to the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
In view of the legal
opinion given by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), perhaps this bill could be allowed to stand. I do not think there will be any difficulty in getting the two railways to agree to 99 years instead of 999.

maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: If the minister will recommend that it be made 999 years, I will withdraw my objection. Will he go on record to that effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADIAN NORTHERN ONTARIO RAILWAY COMPANY AND THE CAMPBELLFORD, LAKE ONTARIO AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
In my opinion the agreement should stand for 999 years.
Amendment (Mr. Munn) withdrawn.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways) moved the second reading of Bill No. 25, to ratify and confirm an agreement respecting the joint use by His Majesty and the commissioners of the Transcontinental railway of certain tracks and premises of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at Quebec.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Morand in the chair.
On section 1-Agreement and supplementary agreement ratified.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: This bill is merely to confirm an arrangement which has been in existence since 1915 between the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways. The two railways jointly use the terminal and this bill is to carry on the agreement for 99 years.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
Would the minister have
any objection to postponing the consideration of this bill until such time as the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) is in his place? I know he has something to say on it and in all probability I shall have some objections to make. I might point out to the minister that I think he was mistaken a few days ago when he said the former agreement was for 999 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
I did not say that; I
said that the previous bill, the one with which we have just been dealing, was for 999 years.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
I took it from Hansard
where the minister said that the former agreement was for 999 years. He then made a correction in Hansard to the same effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
My hon. friend is wrong.
We were dealing with the three bills in the same order as we dealt with them to-day. When we came to this bill my hon. friend asked me if it was for 99 years. I said yes, and that the previous one was for 999 years. I said that that should be long enough, but Hansard put it in as 99 years and made the statement appear foolish. I wanted to correct the statement and make it clear that I was referring to the previous bill, not the previous agreement.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
The original agreement between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Transcontinental Railway was made in 1915. The Transcontinental was represented by the late Hon. Frank Cochrane, but I cannot find

out just at present who represented the Canadian Pacific. Considerable discussion took place in Quebec at that time, as it was understood that the Transcontinental would have a passenger terminus of its own. This agreement came rather as a surprise to the people of Quebec. I notice the new agreement was dated January 1, 1930, yet it appears to have been signed at a much later date. One of the signatories is R. J. Manion, who was not Minister of Railways in January, 1930. Apparently this agreement was left on his doorstep, so to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
I should like my hon.
friend to let me know what other lines he would like information upon. Each one of these agreements comprise thirty or more pages and naturally I cannot familiarize myself with all the details. Generally speaking, in dealing with bills of this sort I take the attitude that the two railways have come to a decision satisfactory to both and are merely asking parliament to ratify the agreement because the law says that that must be done. If my hon. friend has any other suggestions to make I should like to hear them and then I can move that the bill stand.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
Who are the commissioners
of the Transcontinental railway at the present time? I see the minister signs as commissioner.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: I am the commissioner.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: Are there any others?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: No.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
When the minister entered
into this agreement did he do so on the advice of the Canadian National Railways or did he do so as commissioner of the Transcontinental railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
The Canadian National
Railways handles the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental railways. As minister, I act as commissioner in place of the old commissioners of the earlier days. I act on the advice of the Canadian National and sign as commissioner of the National Transcontinental.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
Was this agreement submitted to the officers of the Canadian National Railways?
Mr. MANION; Yes.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
And the minister signed on
the advice of those officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
Yes.

Supply-Fisheries

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: The former agreement signed by the Hon. Mr. Cochrane was made on behalf of the crown. At that time the Canadian National Railways was operated directly by the Minister of Railways; if I may express it so, he was acting in a political capacity whereas at the present time he acts merely as a figure head for the railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: That is correct. At the present time the minister acts entirely on the advice of the management of the Canadian National Railways who operate the National Transcontinental on behalf of the government as part of the national system. I am associated with this in no way except merely to act as commissioner on the advice of the management.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
Pool trains are being run
out of Quebec over the Canadian Pacific tracks only. There will be very few if any Canadian National passenger trains running from this station. This agreement was made in 1930, at which time there were at least three Canadian National passenger trains running out of this station and using the facilities, the tracks and so on. I have not had an opportunity of going into the details of the agreement, but it appears to me that perhaps it might be advisable to modify the agreement so that the burden of the Canadian National Railways would not be quite so heavy.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
Of course the Canadian
National had every opportunity to advise me that they wished some modification, but apparently they did not.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
The pool trains started on
March 11.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: I appreciate that the agreement was made! some time ago. In the absence of my hon. friend a few days ago the hon. member for Quebec East asked a question in regard to the pool trains.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: I was in the house; I heard it.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: Well, that explains the pooling from the standpoint of the Canadian National Railways. However, in view of my hon. friend's remarks I shall gladly put his side of the question before the Canadian National, because I think, had they desired the changes, they should have advised me inasmuch as these bills, they knew, were still in the preliminary stages. Before the bill comes up again I will place before them the suggestions made by my hon. friend, and I shall be glad if he will tell me of any further suggestions he has to offer.

maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext: I have none at the moment, but if aDy occur to me I will inform the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: USE OF CANADIAN PACIFIC TRACKS AND PREMISES AT QUEBEC
speechtext:
I shall be glad to have the information. In the meantime I move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.

Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bury in the chair.
Fisheries

building fishways and clearing rivers, $6,000.
Where was this money spent?

speakeroldname: Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Acting Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It was spent in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia.

Since the building of the St. Andrews locks on the Red river in Manitoba the people have been unable to catch fish. The Red river runs practically north, in the opposite direction to most of the rivers in that part of the country, and in the early days we were able to catch catfish, goldeyes, pickerel and various other kinds of fish. This meant a good deal to the people living along the Red river, but since the building of the locks the fish do not come up the river to spawn. I would ask the minister to take this matter up with his officials to ascertain whether the fishways are really modern, so as to allow the passage of fish up the river to spawn. I understand that the fish caught in the Red river are lazy; they do not go up these fishways. The minister might find out whether it is possible to improve these fishways to facilitate the passage of the fish up the river.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The fisheries being administered by the provincial authorities in Manitoba, I suggest that the hon. gentleman get in touch with the provincial government, who would in turn communicate with the Department of Railways and Canals, and require from that department the construction of fishways and ladders. Nevertheless I shall be pleased to look into the matter and see what the exact situation is.
Supply-Fisheries

I would call the attention of the minister to an anomaly that exists in our section of the country. Three large newsprint and sulphite mills are operating on the Abitibi, the Ground Hog and the Metagami rivers, and apparently the chemicals discharged from these mills poison the waters in these rivers. Formerly there was an enormous catch of sturgeon, and there was an excellent market in the United States for caviar from the district, but that is lost because the fish cannot survive in these waters. I do not know whether this is under federal or provincial jurisdiction

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It is under provincial jurisdiction.

Then I will leave it at that. These rivers are partly navigable and I understand that under this item the clearing of rivers can be taken care of. It is a matter of making the water fit for the survival of fish. This is a considerable industry in our section of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If these were tidal waters this matter would be under the jurisdiction of my department.
They are partly tidal.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The tidal part will no doubt come under my department. Has the hon. gentleman ever taken the matter up with the provincial authorities? As regards the part that comes within the jurisdiction of my department, I will make inquiries to see whether the situation can be remedied, because it is undesirable that the waters of rivers should be poisoned in that way.
This vote has been cut down by two-thirds, which is a very considerable reduction, greater than in any other item. As there is need for the work, I think the minister should explain the reduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It is due to the fact that the expenses for such works have been greatly reduced within the last few years. As a matter of fact during this fiscal year, up to December 31 last, we expended only 11,379. Of course these expenditures cannot always be calculated exactly in advance, because sometimes we are called upon to remove obstructions when we did not expect to have to do so, but from the expenditures we made last year, we believe $6,000 will be ample to meet the requirements for next year.

The explanation is contradictory to the announced policy of the department. When I have applied for work to be done in connection with matters of this

character such as clearing streams or building fishways, I have been tbld that the greatest economy had' to be practised because the money was not available. It now appears that $18,000 was available and only around $1,000 spent. Parsimony wholly unjustifed has been shown by the department. I have, if not willingly, at least acquiesced when I have been told that no money was available, whereas it now appears that ample -money was available but the department neglected the work to which I called attention.
The minister says that expenditures last year amount to $1,300. How many applications did he have for spending money in building new fishways or clearing streams?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We have investigated every case reported to the department, but as my hon. friend knows, fishways are built by the owners themselves and not by the department. The department contributes only in certain cases, and as a rule the construction of fishways is done at the expense of the owners themselves. The principal work of the department is to remove obstructions when we are called upon to do so. As a matter of fact we have answered any call that has been made uipon us and we have given satisfaction at that little expense.
No, I protest; that is not correct.

I quite agree that the building of new fishways is something which the owner of the dam is supposed to look after, but the minister admits the department can help to build new dams or arrange to tear down old ones. The minister of course has not answered my question. I should like to know how many applications the department had last year for work of this character. The minister says that all they spent was $1,300. The department might have had applications necessitating the expenditure of $1,000,000. I am simply using round figures as I do not know the amount. How -many applications had the department and what did it do with them? Did it turn them down flat and spend only $1,300 because it wanted to act against the wishes of the persons applying for work to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
' My information is that the department investigated every application that was made to it and when it was found advisable to do the work, it was done.

Supply-Fisheries-C onservation
How many applications were made to the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have not the records under my hand. I have a large list covering work we have done in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia.
There cannot have been very much done if the department spent only $1,300.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, the work of removing obstructions is not very expensive. As will be seen from the amounts expended, it is not very large. On the Tusfcet river, Yarmouth county, we made an expenditure of $568. On the Clyde river, Shelburne county, we made an expenditure of $25.20; on the Mersey river, Queens county, $46.20 and on the Gaspereau river, Kings county, $89.51. I am informed that we have done what was reasonable. If my hon. friend can supply me with the name of any place where we should have done something which was not done, I shall be pleased to inquire and to do what is reasonable under the circumstances.

I am afraid, instead of my
writing the minister and suggesting certain work should be done at a certain place, my experience is that the only way to get work done by the department is to protest against it. If I reported that certain work should not be done in a certain river, the minister and his officials would likely have that work done, so while I appreciate the minister's solicitude in regard to my giving him information, I am afraid I cannot take advantage of his generosity. The minister has not yet answered my question. What I asked was this: In addition to the work done at an expenditure of $1,300, how many applications were made and from whom were they received?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I have already told
my hon. friend that I cannot give the information because I have not all the files with me.

I would suggest then that
the item stand until we get the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Let the item stand.
Item stands.
To assist in the conservation and development of the deep sea fisheries and the demand for fish, $85,000.

What is the meaning of
the expression " the demand for fish"? Is that to assist in marketing?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Yes, to increase the
demand.

How much was spent last
year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
During the present
fiscal year prior to December 31, last we spent $46,411 and prior to the end of February we had spent around $50,000.
To secure better markets, I mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
No, on the whole
item.

Can the minister divide
that and tell us how much was spent for securing better markets?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The expenditure made to increase the demand for fish has not been very large. As my hon. friend knows, we have used the services of Mrs. Spencer, an outstanding specialist in cooking fish. She has been going all over the country the year round and has done a splendid work. In parts of the country where the population was mostly French wre had an interpreter working in cooperation with Mrs. Spencer.

I am prepared to commend the work done by the lady in question, but that is directed to increasing the use of fish at home. Was any of this sum expended for the opening of markets abroad, and if so, how much?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: That would pertain to another department, that of Trade and Commerce. All over the country we are trying to improve the quality of our fish so that the fish sent to markets abroad shall be of first class quality. We think that is the best means of increasing our exports of fish.
How is the minister trying to improve the quality of fish for shipment to foreign markets? Would he also give a detailed statement of how the $46,000 was spent last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: We seek by educational work and by the enforcement of rigid regulations to ensure that the fish shall be properly packed and canned and sent abroad in first class condition. The fisheries inspectors are being qualified to give instruction in methods, and it has been found necessary to have a thoroughly qualified man devote his whole time to such work, one who can be available to help the fishery officers if needed. We have a special officer known as the promoter of proper fish curing who has done valuable work in that respect.

What is his name?

Supply-Fisheries-Conservation

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: George Earl, and he has assistants.

I have heard of this gentleman, but I have never come in contact with him. Where is he? What does he do? How does he earn his salary? What is the minister paying him for? What are the officials in Ottawa telling him to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: During the season of 1933-34 this man worked chiefly in Prince Edward Island, Guysborough and Richmond counties in Nova Scotia, and the Magdalen islands. Six assistants were employed at times to help him. This class of work is proving highly beneficial, and the department is finding it difficult to keep up with the requests for his services from different localities.
Did he ever get out to British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No.
Who are the assistants, and how are they appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: They are all appointed by the civil service commission. Does my hon. friend desire the names? The promoter's name is G. R. Earl, at a salary of $2,520, less ten per cent of course.
That is too bad.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
His assistants are
P. Mercier, William Mercier, W. H. Casiboom, Earle McRae, A. Wilson and B. Latham, at a salary of $4.50 per day each.

In this item is mentioned the development of deep sea fisheries. The minister has just told the committee he spent $46,000 last year for the advertising of fish and so on. I assume under this item some money should have been spent during the last two years in the investigation of fishing possibilities in Hudson bay and James bay, but if my information is correct the department has not made any move in that direction, although the present Minister of Finance, when he was Minister of Marine and fisheries, almost promised the committee to enlarge on the inquiry that was made in the summer of 1930. In our section we are not satisfied with the results of that inquiry. As far as the work done in 1930 is concerned, we believe it was well done but we think it should have been enlarged. Only a few days were spent in the whole Hudson bay area, comprising nearly 700,000 square miles of water, after which the statement was made that there were no salt water fish in all that great expanse. The minister was not very

definite, but at any rate he created the impression that further investigation would be made. I am not going to read the report of the investigation made by the 1930 expedition, but I state frankly that that report is not satisfactory to the people interested in that section of the country. We maintain that there are salt water fish in those waters. It is true that in the estuaries of the rivers running into Hudson bay there are fresh water fish, which at certain times of the year migrate into Hudson bay and James bay. Perhaps the minister will say that on such a question they cannot carry the investigation further, but I know from reports received from people familiar with the situation in that area that there are salt water fish in Hudson bay and James bay. To corroborate my statement I will read part of a good report that was made by W. R. Maher, an engineer of the T. & N.O. Railway who knows well that northern part of Ontario and Quebec including James bay and Hudson bay. This report was published in the North Bay Nugget of October 26, 1932. He says:
From a tourist standpoint the east coast offers adventure, exploration, new fishing grounds and bird life in abundance for gun and camera. Charlton island could be made a desirable base for canoe or motor boat trips along the coast which could be made under the protection of islands. Sea trout are found in such numbers and of such excellence as to alone establish the James bay as one of the leading fishing resorts of the continent.
That statement comes from a man well versed in all that pertains to those northern waters. I believe he is known to the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Railways. Mr. Maher would not have made that report unless he was sure of his statement from personal inquiry on the ground.
A little further on in the report, describing a trip he made in James bay and Hudson bay waters, he says:
Hundreds of seals were seen swimming and resting on the ice. Gulls, guillemots and terns were evidently feeding, but only jellyfish were seen.
Anyone familiar with salt water fishing knows that there would be no seals unless there were salt water fish. Seals would not come all the way down to James bay to feed on the fresh water fish; they would get most of their feeding on salt water fish. Only, a few days ago I was talking with Captain Bernier, who is known in every section of Canada for his voyages of exploration in Canadian Arctic waters. He tells me that every summer quite a number of Scandinavian schooners spend the whole fishing season in the Hudson strait and the Ungava

Supply-F isheries-C onservation
section fishing for cod, although he tells me there are no banks, but on the eastern side of Hudson bay there would be good grounds for cod fishing. Again Mr. Maher says:
On entering the river a school of white whales, several hundred in number, were seen playing about at the end of Manitunuk sound.
That would seem to prove that there must be some salt water fish in that great expanse of water. I do not know how true it is, but in our section it is said that the government do not want to develop our fishing industry because it will provide very keen competition for the fisheries of the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. We do not want to believe that, but that is what is being said. Geographically speaking, we are in the centre of Canada, and with the extension of the railway to salt water we are in a position to give a thirty-six hour service for fresh and salt water fish to such markets as Toronto and Montreal, and even the United States. We do not want to attribute ulterior motives to other sections of the country, but I am firmly convinced that the government would be well advised to continue the investigation which was started in 1930. I need not refer further to that inquiry, but the fact remains that they only actually fished in the Hudson bay for less than one day, and any man familiar with that expanse of water will readily understand that it was impossible in that time to cover the territory properly. We maintain that a trawler or schooner should remain there for the winter months in order to have a whole season in which to investigate the situation the following year.
I have here a report which was made following investigations into the fisheries of Hudson and James bays and tributary waters in 1914 by C. B. Melvill, A. R. M. Lower and N. A. Comeau. I believe this report will corroborate what I have said with regard to the fisheries of Hudson bay. With reference to codfish, at page 24 the report states:
Cod are known to occur in Hudson bay. A few schooners from St. Johns fish in Hudson straits and Ungava bay every year. There would apparently be, therefore, no reason why these fish should not exist in larger quantities than have yet been found.
The investigation of 1930 was not lengthy enough to cover the fisheries of Hudson bay very thoroughly. Speaking of the different species of fish that have been found on the west coast of Hudson bay, the report goes on to say:
The other species of the west coast are not of a great deal of economic importance; rock-cod occur in the bay and it is said that the true cod does also-
The true cod does exist also, but no investigation of the west coast was made in 1930.
-but there is no record of a single specimen of either of them ever having been found on the west coast.
That would corroborate the statement I made a few moments ago, that the east coast of Hudson bay should have been thoroughly investigated, and I believe the investigation should be continued. The report goes on to say:
Besides the strictly fish wealth, there are other forms of marine life possessed of considerable value: one such as the white whale, another is the seal. The former occurs in great numbers and as he is quite valuable for his oil-of which he yields 100 gallons each, it may be expected that an industry founded on his products will develop as soon as the market is brought near enough to the place of production. The seal is not the fur seal but its hide makes extraordinary waterproof bags, hoots, gun covers, and so on.
Further on in this report they touch on the question of the whitefish that exists in the estuaries of these rivers. I need not name the great rivers that pour their waters into Hudson bay; I believe the names are familiar to every member of this house. Everyone is familiar with the wonderful quality of whitefish, and I believe an industry could 'be built up comparable to the goldeye industry in Manitoba. It is a well known fact that in these estuaries there are unlimited numbers of whitefish during several months of the year, as well as in James bay and Hudson bay. In this report they have this to say with regard to transportation:
When the Hudson bay railway is opened, it will be possible to get the products of the smaller bay out to the cities of the west in the course of a few days, and then we shall expect to see greater use made of them. Such a traffic will require substantial fishing tugs, quite independent of wind and tide, for these latter are the great bugbear of all traffic carried on with the old fashioned craft.
That statement applies even more forcibly at the present time for the very good reason that now the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway has been extended to tidewater at James bay, and we are in a position to give wonderful service in the distribution of fish not only to central Canada but also to the United States.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that I have built up a strong case, and I fervently hope the government will find it possible under this item of 855,000, of which only 846,000 is spent in connection with the advertising of fish in this country, to carry on that investigation into the fisheries of Hudson bay and James

Supply-Interior

bay. In our part of the country we are quite willing to go half way at all times; I believe we have shown in the past that we are not critical of advances made in other sections of Canada, but I repeat that we are not satisfied with the investigation that was carried on in 1930. We were satisfied with the work actually accomplished, but we were not satisfied with the small amount of work done. I hope the minister will be in a position to tell the committee that under this item, and not later than the year 1935, his department will find it possible to make a very thorough inquiry that will satisfy our people.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certain correspondence has passed between the Department of the Interior and the department concerned in Ontario in connection with this matter. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may say that the wolf bounty has been discontinued also in the provinces.
I am not surprised at that.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But the hon. member is surprised at this.

I am surprised at the action of the minister. I am not at all surprised that the provinces should reduce the bounties because they are reducing everything. If the game are to be preserved, something will have to be paid for the extermination of the wolves. The tendency at present is for the wolves to keep southward so that the menace from the wolves that the trappers will not poison and kill in the provinces will not be so great in the north. But I honestly think it is a mistake for the department to discontinue these bounties.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member may be correct; I suppose time will answer that question, but may I say that the provinces took this action first and the hon. member will, I think, be aware of the great temptation there would be to those who were hunting and trapping, say in the northern parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, having slain a number of wolves and coyotes, to take 
them over into the territories and collect the bounty from the Dominion government. Further, as the hon. member is well aware, formerly we paid the bounty and the government retained the fur. The hunters and trappers will now have the sale of their furs, and the prices, I am glad to say, of all furs have advanced considerably. The question of decreasing the numbers will rest now, as it did before, with the individual trapper, and if he can secure for his fur as great an amount as he used to receive in bounty from the Dominion government, I think the objection of the hon. member will be met.

That may
be, but the Dominion government under both parties has gone to considerable expense in trying to exterminate wolves. It is a great thing they have been exterminated around Ottawa, but they are a growing menace in the northwest and I am afraid that the minister will find them getting into his parks. If the provinces discontinue the bounty, we shall have the same trouble as we had in the past. The wolf family seems to increase very fast and there is no doubt that they play the very mischief with deer. The result will be that throughout the whole northern section deer will be exterminated. While I agree with the minister that the price of fur has increased, it is rather difficult, as he knows, to trap a wolf. A trapper can make much more money by trapping other kinds of game than by trapping wolves, and the fact that he had the assurance of $20 per pelt was some incentive to him to get busy to try to exterminate them. Therefore I regret that the government have changed their policy in regard to the bounty on wolves, and I may say that I think the provinces have also made a veiy serious mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Like the hon. member
who has just taken his seat, I am well aware of the value of wild life to the dominion, especially that which inhabits our great national parks. Special and very strict instructions were sent out to our wardens during this past year to destroy the predatory animals in the parks, and I receive monthly reports in regard to the numbers killed. I am happy to tell the committee that there are no evidences this year of any great number of predatory animals in our national parks. I feel that the objection of the hon. member is met by the fact that owing to the increase in the price of fur those who formerly received the bounty will now receive as much from the sale of fur as they received

Supply-Interior
from the bounty. As a matter of fact complaints reached us that we were not paying enough by way of bounty-that they could get more out of the sale of the fur.

There is a feature that I think has been overlooked here, as it was in the province of Manitoba. When Manitoba was paying bounty for the destruction of coyotes the Indians would go out in the spring and hunt up the dens and kill the pups, because the young pups brought them as much bounty as the mature animal. I speak with special relation to the sheep industry:	I have good reason to know the
damage that wolves may do in a flock of sheep; for I think I can say without exaggeration that I lost about S200 worth of lambs last summer from wolves. The fact that the Indians got $2 for destroying the pups was a great incentive to hunt them. We must remember that a wolf may do a tremendous amount of damage between the time it is a pup and the time it is mature enough to be trapped for its fur. I know that in Manitoba the bounty was discontinued, without an understanding of that fact. At our United Farmers' convention we had occasion to bring it to the notice of some of those who had advised the Manitoba government in the matter, and they evidently were not aware of the situation. I know that in my own district, and I presume it is the same wherever there are Indians and wolves, the Indians would hunt the young ones and kill them before they had a chance to do any damage. So the fact that the price of fur has gone up sufficiently to increase the incentive to trap the mature animals does not by any means meet the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was dealing with the
situation as it exists in the Northwest Territories. The complaint of the hon. member is, I think, well taken, but it applies to the provincial jurisdiction, not to that of the dominion. I was merely replying to the objections raised by the former Minister of the Interior in regard to the situation in the Northwest Territories, where, as I think the hon. member knows, there are no domestic animals.
But the same argument will apply where there are young deer and other game as well as where there are sheep.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In regard to the taking of the animals when they are young, I agree with the hon. member that such might be the case, but as a matter of fact and of record the bounty was practically all paid on mature animals. The wolves and coyotes
were taken at the time of year when the ordinary hunting operations were going on and other fur-bearing animals were taken as well. I am well aware of the very great damage which can be done to a flock of sheep by either wolves, coyotes or the domestic dog, which is just as bad as the wolf when it takes to predatory habits.

There is mention in another item of Wood Buffalo park. Will the minister explain where this park is situated, when it was established, its size, the extent of its development, and the use to which it has been put during the last four years?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: While my official is looking up part of the information asked for I shall say that Wood Buffalo park lies partly in the Northwest Territories and partly in Alberta, the greater part being in the province. The main purpose it serves is that of a game sanctuary. To the best of our information, it is inhabited by some thousands of wood buffalo as well as fur bearing animals, beaver and all other fur bearers that are indigenous to the northern part of Alberta and the territories. I have not information at hand as to the year in which it was established, but I may be able to get it in a moment.

speechtext: The estimated populatior in 1930 was 7,103. That included all Canadian Eskimos, but was only an estimate. The latest census, that of 1931, which we feel is quite accurate, showed 4,670, but that does not include those living in the northern part of Quebec.
They are about as slow as some political parties we know.

I hope the minister is not reducing the number of wardens patrolling the buffalo park. Has he the same number of men there?

speechtext: There are at present ten wardens, which I believe is an increase over the number of a few years ago.

speechtext: No buffalo have been taken north within the last three years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Between 1925 and 1928
there were 6,673 of the animals taken from Wainwright to the Wood buffalo park, and at that time there were approximately 1,500 at that point.

Are experiments
being continued in the crossing of buffalo with domestic cattle?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I believe that experiment

Has the minister now
the information for which I asked?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not the date of
the establishment of the park, but if the hon. gentleman will repeat his questions I will give him the rest of the information.

My questions were as
to the exact location of Wood buffalo park, when it was established, its size, its development and the use to which it has been put during the last four years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I explained a few
moments ago, Mr. Chairman, the park lies principally within the province of Alberta, with a small portion in the Mackenzie district of the northwest territories. It contains 17.300 square miles, of which 3,625 are in the northwest territories, the remainder being in Alberta. The sole purpose for which it is used is that of a buffalo preserve and a game sanctuary, with the exception that Indians and halfbreeds are allowed, under permit, to carry on hunting and trapping of fur bearing animals in that area.

The minister has given

speechtext:

Supply-Interior
