speechtext: No, but I hope they will be very shortly.

There is just a question I should like to ask; it has to do with the constituency of Pontiac. I do not see the hon. member who represents that riding here, but I am his neighbour and I should like to bring it up. This has to do with some Indians who are in the parish of Timiskaming, on the Quebec side. I believe representations have been made to the minister to the effect that quite a number of Indians occupy a large area of land which is very well suited for agriculture. I have personal knowledge that very few of those Indians are interested in agriculture; in fact only two or three of them cultivate a very small acreage. I am informed that the federal government has to supply those Indians with wood during the summer and winter months, because there is hardly a stick of wood left there. A good many people interested in that section of the country desire to have that land given or sold to the province of Quebec in order that white people may settle there. Let me repeat that these Indians are not interested in agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will permit me to interrupt. He will realize that we are now dealing with the Department of the Interior; I shall be pleased to take up the matter when the estimates of the Indian department are under consideration.

I notice some of this
money is for the maintenance of hospitals. How many hospitals are there, and how many medical men are maintained?

There are eight hospitals, one at Fort Smith, one at Fort Resolution, one at Hay River, one at Fort Simpson, two at Aklavik, one at Chesterfield and one at Pangnirtung, which is situated in Baffin Land.
With one medical man at each place?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Paid either entirely by the Department of the Interior or jointly with the Indian Department.

I notice that part of this money is to be used for the exploration, investigation and development of natural resources. In view of the mining development that is taking place in Canada, this part of the appropriation will serve a very useful purpose. May I ask approximately what part of this S195,000 is to be used for this purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is an item in the estimates of $23,300 which is appropriated for the annual trip of a boat sailing from Montreal or Sydney, Nova Scotia, to the northern latitudes, and carrying supplies for our hospitals and the personnel of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police located at various posts in the territories. We endeavour to send on that expedition as many scientific men as we can, and frequently the other departments cooperate with us to that end. It takes the boat about three months to make the trip, calling at various points in Baffin Land and on the shores of the Hudson bay, and at certain islands in the Arctic. In addition to that, valuable exploratory work is carried on by the geological survey of the Mines department. In connection with the maps which we were discussing under the vote for the topographical survey a few moments ago, the aerial photographic work is carried on by the Department of National Defence.
May I digress for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to say that if members of the committee can spare the time for a visit to the topographical survey, they will find an inspection of the aerial photographs and maps of that area in the Northwest Territories in which mineral development has been so great in the last two years well worth their while, and I am sure they will agree that their time was well spent. Immense strides have been made in the last few years in the taking of aerial photographs and, perhaps more important still, in the interpretation of those photographs by men who have made a scientific study of that subject. Again I recommend that the members of the committee visit the photographic library of the topographical survey.

I thank the minister for the information that he has given to the committee. He has spoken of scientists going north once a year. Do those scientists come from different departments of the government, and do the universities cooperate in that work?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Macdonald College cooperated with the department last year and sent a man. We also secure the services of government scientists when they can be spared from their work in the departments, notably in the Department of Mines, which has worked very closely with the Department of the Interior in our efforts to investigate the resources of that northern country.

I think this is the proper item, Mr. Chairman, upon which to say a few words with regard to the wild fowl of this country and the possibility of encouraging the
Supply-Interior

establishment of sanctuaries for them in the west. Those who are informed on the question advise me that our wild duck and geese are decreasing at the rate of ten per cent a year. If that is so, these wild fowl will disappear within ten years. This is not a question of importance merely to the sportsman; for these wild fowl are of considerable importance as food to the natives of the far north, who shoot them and have their own refrigerating system for keeping them during the winter until the following spring. Just on the edge of the city of Calgary we have a fairly large bird sanctuary which is maintained by private donations and by the Calgary fish and game association. The expense of maintaining the sanctuary is becoming greater each year, and it has got to the point where private donations will no longer sustain it. We have had the assistance of the minister through his departmental officials in extending the protected area, and very real assistance has been given to the work of the association. However, if the fowl are to be protected by sanctuaries, the encouragement of this means of protection might well be given consideration by the department, with a view' to seeing what measure of assistance can be given to those now actually in existence, and what should be done in establishing new sanctuaries.
The question of maintaining the fowl in the northlands during the winter months is one upon which there are decided differences of opinion. I am sorry to say that our provincial authorities are averse to doing anything to keep the wild fowl from going south. But if no international agreement can be made, and we do not seem to be succeeding very well in that direction, the fact remains that if the estimate of a decrease at the rate of ten per cent a year is correct-and I believe these people know what they are talking about-we are facing a serious problem in regard to our wild fowl. The only thing we can do under the circumstances is to establish sanctuaries of our own, and encourage and assist those now in existence so that we may keep our wild fowl in our owrn land.
In addition to what I have already said, the feed which is used in our sanctuary in Calgary is purchased from the large elevators and contains many weed seeds which have been sent out from the elevators to the farms for purposes of feed for stock, thereby spreading weeds far and wide. So that by using this feed from our grain elevators, our sanctuaries are helping to eradicate one of the great scourges of our western land. I bring this matter before the minister for his consideration because it is one of considerable

importance not only to our fish and game association but also to those living in the far north whose welfare is a matter of concern to the department over which the minister presides.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member has
opened up a large question, one in which I take a deep personal interest. The matter could, however, be more properly discussed under the item which includes an amount for the administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act. I will read the hon. member's remarks in Hansard to-morrow, and when this item is before the committee I shall be pleased to discuss the matter.
Does this vote cover the natural resources branch, or is this branch now non-existent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is not the vote.
Is there any item which covers that branch? It has done splendid work in the past and I should like to know if it has been moved to some other department, or if it is non-existent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. member refers to the national development bureau. This branch has been discontinued as part of the Department of the Interior, but some of the work which it carried on is now being performed by the departments of Mines, Trade and Commerce, and Interior.

In the past this branch did much work of great value. It never received the public credit to which it was entitled. It was small, but its contact with the industrial development boards of the various cities resulted in great improvement in many sections of the country. If this branch is not in the minister's department there is no use in my discussing it at this time. I have not been able to find out in just what department the branch is located, but if the minister will tell me when the item comes up I shall be prepared to say something on it.

amount provided for advertising is very small.

Has the minister that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

Is this fund periodically examined on an actuarial basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes; the fund is audited by the auditor general's department every quarter.
That does not quite answer the question. I wish to know whether on an actuarial basis the annuities are in a sound condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There are conflicting views with regard to the question whether or not one can describe these annuities as being on a sound basis. All governments since the act was passed in 1908 have taken the attitude, and I am inclined to think properly so, that these annuities should be sold on the basis of the government absorbing the cost of administration, because the annuities themselves are limited to $1,200, and the legislation was designed primarily to give an opportunity to those of modest income to take advantage of the annuities during the years when they were able to save something. I have heard the question discussed both ways by actuaries representing the annuities branch and by actuaries of companies as to whether these annuities were sold at a more favourable or a less favourable rate than those sold by private companies. I am not an actuary, but I am inclined to think, after listening to both sides, that they are sold at a slightly more favourable rate than the annuities sold by private companies.
How does the cost of writing this business compare with that of the best insurance companies for the same amount of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The actuaries of the department contend that the cost is almost in equation. They will not go so far as to say that it is completely in equation with the best annuity companies. I think that both sides rather rely upon their expertness with figures, but I am inclined to the view that these annuities are sold at a lower cost than the annuities sold by some of the better private companies.

How is the business collected? Is a commission paid or is it done by the permanent officials of the department?

Supply-Labour-Annuities Act

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The hon. member means, how are the commissions paid?
Yes, if any.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: They are paid out of the consolidated revenue fund, and appropriate entries are made into the annuities fund to take care of them from time to time.
What is the basis of the commissions?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The hon. member will forgive me if I am unable to go into details in matters that have to do with higher mathematics, because it is a good many years since I had to struggle with such questions. On an immediate, single payment deferred annuity- that is, one deferred, from one to five years -the commission is one per cent; deferred more than five years, two per cent. The maximum commission payable in respect of an application or applications for the purchase of immediate or single payment deferred annuity or annuities received from any one purchaser shall be $100; that is to say, it is limited to that amount. On deferred annual payment annuities, where payment is to be completed in one year, the commission is one per cent; where payment is to be completed in two years, two per cent for two years; where payment is to be completed in three years, three per cent for two years; where payment is to be completed in four years, four per cent for two years. There is a maximum commission payable in respect of an application for the purchase of a deferred annual payment annuity or annuities received from any one purchaser, of $125, and I am told by the officers of the department-and I believe it to be correct-that there is a higher maximum paid by the best private companies than is paid by the department to its commission agents.

I agree with the minister
that the act is one of the best that has been put on the statute books for the benefit of the low wage earners, and I congratulate him on the improvement shown, especially in the last year. It is true that the sale of annuities is increasing, but it is doing so only because of moneys that have been spent in previous years in advertising, bringing the matter before the people. But I have no doubt it is desirable and, I believe, necessary to do such advertising as will acquaint people of small means with the security offered by investment in these annuities and I will bear in mind in that regard the observations made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.

I thank the minister for the information he has given to the committee with regard to the question I asked. I think there is a direct relation between the amount of money, every dollar the department ever spent on advertising, and the amount of annuities sold to the Canadian people. I believe, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has just said, the department is now reaping the benefit of constructive advertising in past years. I am sure we all know the statement in the Good Book: "Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days." That is exactly the situation we have in this case. The hard publicity work was done in past years and the department is reaping the benefit from year to year. If the best work is to be done in the future and the postmasters of Canada are to sell the amount of annuities expected of them, this publicity must be carried on. Might I ask the minister what his policy with regard to this publicity is to be? Has he made up his mind as to what it will be next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Yes; the government's
policy with respect to advertising is to carry on such well directed advertising as is required to bring before those who may be interested in the small annuities the plain facts and the benefits that will flow from the investment of their money during the time they are capable of earning to take care of them in the misfortunes and misadventures that may come to them in the twilight of their lives. That is the policy.
In view of the fact that annuities seem to be sold by the government cheaper than by private companies, does the minister expect to increase the selling price of government annuities?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: If my memory serves me correctly, the annuities bill was first introduced in the Senate in 1908 by the late Sir Richard Cartwright and subsequently sponsored in this house by the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. While I have not had opportunity for many years to read their statements and remarks at that time, I believe that the principle upon which the then government embarked on the sale of annuities was primarily to provide small annuities for people of very modest means, to encourage them in thrift and the adoption of a course calculated to build up for themselves a reserve fund for their later life. Having that in view I believe it was the opinion of those men, with which I do not quarrel, that it was desirable that the government should absorb the cost of administration, which in connection with annuities issued by private companies of course is borne by the annuitant, together with some profit. I think perhaps there is no better activity in which the government can be engaged than that of devoting some money from the consolidated revenue fund to making measurably attractive this sort of investment for people who have not too much of this world's goods and who are earnestly striving in a thrifty way to make provision for their future years.

The minister spoke of
an annuity being a first class investment for a citizen to have in the twilight of life. Can he give the committee the age limit at which an annuity investment is most profitable, considering all circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

Supply-Labour-Conciliation Act
me to advise anyone at what age they should start to save for old age. But from my limited experience in finance I would say, start to save money at as early an age as possible.
And keep right on at it.

I would like to raise a question under this item which perhaps has not been raised here for some time. I have no doubt that many hon. members have been amazed and shocked at the revelations brought out by the * committee dealing with mass buying and price spreads. The low wages which have been paid in too many industries show that the government ought to attempt, in connection with its contracts, to see that fair wage provisions are properly lived up to. In calling the attention of the minister to this matter I do' not want him to feel that I am attempting any personal reflection, but it has come to my knowledge that contracts which have been entered into by the government have been sublet and then sublet again, and the goods manufactured under the worst possible conditions right here in Canada. I realize that when the government let con-

tracts they include some kind of fair wage clause, and if there is not a fair wage clause I suppose they provide for the going rates of pay in the district in which the goods are to be produced. I have in mind one contract let by the government which was subsequently sublet and then sublet again to a third and possibly a fourth party, and the girls working on this contract were earning, I am told by reliable people, $2 or $3 a week-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. member, but I may tell him that purchases made now by this government have included in the contract a clause plainly stipulating that the laws with respect to wages in effect in the province in which the contract is to be carried out must be observed, and the eight hour day. I do not want the hon. member to feel that I am taking an attitude calculated to close off discussion of this most important matter, but I would draw the attention of the chair to the fact that the topic to which the hon. member is addressing himself is now being reviewed by a select committee of this house, of which I believe the hon. gentleman is himself a member. While I confess that my knowledge of the rules is perhaps not as comprehensive as it should be, I believe there is a rule that when a matter is under consideration by such a committee it should not be the subject of argument and review in the house.

As to the point of order raised by the minister, I am now dealing with a question relating to the enforcement of fair wages by the Department of Labour. I am not attempting to discuss a question that is before the committee, but am trying to find out what action the Department of Labour has taken to see that the fair wage clause in government contracts is properly observed. I do not think there is any relation between the matter referred to by the minister and that which I am now discussing. I do not know whether the minister wants to press his point of order, but I shall not pursue the matter much further because the minister has now given the assurance that the matter is being properly looked after by the Department of Labour. May I ask the minister this question? Supposing it is found that these regulations have been violated by contractors or subcontractors; what action is taken by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
If it were shown that a contractor was guilty of a breach of the contract and was not complying with its terms the government would have two courses open

Supply-Labour-Conciliation Act
to it. One would be to cancel the contract; the other would be to have the conciliation and fair wage officers investigate the situation. If it were found, as in the hypothetical case to which the hon. member has made reference, that fair wages were not being paid, then without hesitation the Department of Labour would notify the other department concerned and ask that the money due that contractor be withheld until the terms of the contract were carried out and fair wages paid.

The case to which I am referring is not hypothetical by any means; I am quite prepared to give the names and details in full. Supposing a contract is let by the government; the contractor sublets that contract and the subcontractor lets it to a third party. Who is to be held responsible for the enforcement of the contract as it was entered into between the government and the first contractor?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I assume the hon. member means who will be held responsible by the government. In the absence of anything of a special nature to the contrary the legal position would be that the government was dealing only with the first contractor. Obviously there is no obligation on the government to follow it through afterwards, but if it is made to appear that the main contractor, either himself or through the agency of subcontractors, has been guilty of procuring a breach of a contract, the position does not give rise to any very serious difficulty, because the money can be held back upon the facts being made known.

Then may I just pursue the matter a little further. Where there are no fair wTage laws, as in the part of the country I have in mind, the prevailing rates apply, and of course these vary. There are some districts where they are probably all sweatshop rates, or the contract may be let in a small place that has only one factory, which may pay extremely low wages. Those wages may amount to only one half or one quarter of the minimum rate in similar lines of industry elsewhere. I think the government should be a model employer of labour and should insist in the contracts it lets for government supplies that proper rates of wages should be paid. I know that under some contracts it is easy for the contractor to get out of paying fair wages by paying the going rate in the district concerned; that may be only $3, $4 or $5 a week, while if the goods were produced under decent conditions the wages might be from $12 to $15 a week. I hope the government intend to clean up this class of sweatshop, in
view of the fact that lately they have come into such prominence, but I think the government should give a lead by seeing that goods produced under government contracts are produced under the best possible conditions.
There is one matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee.
I wonder if my hon. friend would allow the minister to give his viewpoint on the question I have raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I can only repeat the
point I raised a short time ago, with respect to this whole matter being before a special committee of this house. No one in this chamber knows better than my hon. friend the difficulties that confront the federal government in connection with wages paid in sweat shops and so on. I have told my hon. friend of the attitude taken by this government with respect to contracts that have been let; at least it gives some leadership to the various provinces letting similar government contracts, but [DOT] of course that does not indicate the full extent of the influence exerted by this government. In this way it indicates, at least, to industry, to manufacturers, wholesale buyers and others, the viewpoint of this government, and I hope the viewpoint of all provincial governments. But again I say that the hon. gentleman should not ask me to anticipate what action this government will or may take when I am sure every hon. member in this chamber, whether or not he is a supporter of the government, would prefer to have the benefit of the conclusions and recommendations arrived at by the committee now sitting, of which the hon. gentleman is a member. Certainly I should like to have them before I make any observations, and I think it would be entirely unfair to that committee and perhaps just as unfair to myself to ask me to make any such statement now.

I cannot agree with the minister. We are now discussing the policy of the government and this comes up on the estimates. The prevailing rate of wages in an industry may be only two or three dollars a week, as my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) has said. In my judgv ment the government has a distinct responsibility in connection with the wages paid under contracts let by the government. The minister has said the government has cancelled contracts, but I should like the minister to tell us of any contracts that have been cancelled. Frankly I think the policy of the government is absolutely wrong; it is

Supply-Labour-Conciliation Act
similar to the policy that has been followed by the minimum wage board in Ontario. They sit back and wait until complaints are made, without taking into consideration the dangers which confront the employees if they make complaints. The function of this department is to go out and insist that the conditions of labour under contracts let by the government should be fair and equitable. It is altogether wrong that a member of this house should be able to give instances of sweatshop conditions existing in industry arising out of contracts let by this government.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the federal government has a direct responsibility, which does not cease when they say the prevailing rate of wages is 'being paid. They should insist that a living rate of wages be paid, and when I say a living rate I mean a rate in conformity with living conditions as we understand them in Canada. In the past the policy of the Department of Labour has been absolutely negative in connection with the low wages paid under contracts let by the government. They have sat back and waited until complaints were made. Since they have some knowledge of labour conditions in this country, they must know that unless an organization exists it is well nigh impossible for the employees to make any complaint. In connection with the subletting of these contracts the government should insist that when a contractor tenders it should not be possible for him to sublet the work to another contractor and then have that work sublet to still a third man. The responsibility rests with the government to insist that fair rates of wages be paid in the industry which is concerned with the contract. Arising out of the minister's observations I would ask him if he has knowledge of any contract being cancelled during the past year because the rate of wages did not conform with the regulations of his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I have no information, Mr. Chairman, with respect to any contracts that have been absolutely cancelled, but there is, however, a long list of contracts wherein the officers of the department have investigated, both after complaints and on their own initiative, situations that have come to their notice which in their judgment and in my judgment required investigation. In some instances it was found that there was nothing to support the complaints that were made. In other instances, and there was quite a number of them, adjustments were made where it was found that the contractor was not paying, for instance, the current rate of wages. Those are

matters that are constantly before the officers of the federal department. I can only say to both the hon. members who have just spoken that so far as federal contracts are concerned the federal government will take every possible means to see that in the work carried out for each department of government, living and fair wages are paid. So far as the wage earner is concerned, if he or she is not paid a fair and living wage by manufacturers or by others, wholesalers or anybody else, unless both the employer and the employee happen to be in the same state of financial difficulty at the same time, then I will say that the employer has very little justification for trying to carry on at all.

We are very glad to have
that statement from the minister,

A few minutes ago the
Minister of Labour, speaking of the decrease in the item, said that he hoped less would be spent this year. I hope that his wish will be fulfilled, because it would mean that we would have less labour trouble in Canada. The minister is well aware that there were two or three bushmen's strikes last fall in northern Ontario, and that there is one on even now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Not now?

There is one at Chapleau at the present moment. As I stated in my remarks in the debate on the address, there might have been objections to some of the leaders but I certainly am not in a position to state that the leaders were radical or bolshevik or anything of that kind. There is this one fact that Canada should be seized of, and that is that there were many anomalies in the conditions under which the bushmen and settlers cutting pulpwood were working in Ontario and Quebec, and both provincial governments have seen fit to devise new labour regulations. Where there is smoke there is often fire. The strikes that took place last fall were to a very large extent warranted. I was among the strikers for a number of weeks and I know the conditions. Not later than last week the province of Quebec passed statutes dealing wholly with bushmen and with men engaged in lumbering operations. I have not yet had time to study that legislation, but I have no doubt that it was designed to remedy some of the anomalies that have existed in the past. What is true of northern Quebec is true of northern Ontario.
I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that great credit must be given to the strike leaders, because so far as I know the strikers in places like Kapuskasing, Cochrane, Iroquois Falls and

Supply-Labour-Conciliation Act
Smooth Rock Falls were absolutely well behaved and had the wholehearted support of the citizens in those towns and localities. So after all these leaders must have been good, practical labour men. I know for a positive fact that some of these men belonged to the national and international unions, and in corroboration of what I say let me add that the sulphite and newsprint workers in the big mills at Iroquois Falls and Smooth Rock Falls and Kapuskasing each gave one hour's pay for the upkeep of the strike. If there had been too much radicalism in the leading of the strike it would not have been supported by the national and international laboijr unions. A great amount of good has come from having the situation thus brought so forcibly before the public. But I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the Labour department should take the initiative in a strike of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I can tell the hon. member that the Labour department, acting in conjunction with the department in Ontario, sent out officers to places like Kapuskasing where it was possible to effect conciliation. The hon. member for Ivenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) well knows from his experience how desirable it is that when conciliation officers go into places like that, they should be given the opportunity by those in dispute to bring both parties together. That is the essence of conciliation. Our officers were in places where it was possible to do that. My references the other day were to places in northern Ontario where certain elements were at work which argued and advised and cajoled and did everything possible to keep employer and employee apart, giving no chance to the conciliation officers to operate. The whole basis of efficient conciliation work in industry or anywhere else where there is more than one person concerned, where there are conflcting interests, is to give the opportunity for conciliation to smooth out the difficulties and get everyone as nearly satisfied as humans can be. Our officers were in those places where conciliation was possible, and my reference the other day was to places where, by reason of the activities of certain elements, the efforts of the conciliation officers were rendered impossible.

I greatly appreciate the statement which has just been made by the Minister of Labour. I am aware of the fact that officers of the federal Department of Labour were endeavouring to bring about a settlement of the dispute, and I have never criticized the work which they did. But I still maintain that it is the prerogative of the Labour department, whether of the federal
or the provincial government, to take the initiative, and if the provincial department fails to take it, the federal department should step in. The initiative was taken in the Kapuskasing strike, and the result was that that strike was settled early. I hope the day will soon come, Mr. Chairman, and I am speaking as a citizen who knows something of labour unions and the situation of labour, when we shall find it possible to have one Labour department for all Canada. I am convinced that the Minister of Labour personally wants to bring about conciliation in these strikes, and last fall I found myself in the same position, though on a smaller scale, that he has just described, because the company and the strikers did not appear willing to accept my services in conciliation, taking the view that the settlement of the strike was primarily a provincial matter.
With reference to the minister's allusions on February 26 to the effect that some of the leaders in the Chapleau strike were radicals, I want to say that even if some of the strikers might be inclined to be radical, a lot of credit is due to their leaders for bringing to the attention of the public the anomalies that existed, and some of which still exist in some of these lumbering camps in northern Ontario. Talk of sweatshops and of people being underpaid! I say, Mr. Chairman, that one of the things that should be investigated by the committee on price spreads is the lumbering industry and operating conditions in that industry throughout Canada. They will find real sweatshop conditions; they will find men working to the utmost of their physical ability and receiving only a few cents remuneration. These conditions do not exist in all sections but they are to be found in most. There were reasons for the strike last fall; the men were smarting under injustices. In many cases the settlers were not receiving justice but through their leaders these men were able to bring their case before the Canadian public and legislation is now being enacted which will secure them better treatment.
I should like to make a few remarks in connection with the statement made by the Minister of Labour on January 26. I have in my hand a letter containing nineteen pages. It is very well written and I do not know but I should read it to the committee.
Take it as read.

Some hon. members
may object, but these men have been suffering. They do not know just where to find a solution for their problem. It is stated in



Supply-Labour-Conciliation Act
this letter that certain camps are absolutely filthy and not fit for human habitation. I know that no hon. member would live in them for even half a day.
Were there not conferences with regard to these camps?

Conferences were held
and it is hoped that the situation will be improved. I believe that this committee should realize the situation. The provincial and federal governments should attempt to remedy these conditions. After all, a lumberman, an axeman or a settler is a human being who is just as much entitled to a good living as any hon. member or other citizen of this country. I hope the minister will make it a point to consider this letter and give it the attention it deserves. The gentleman who writes it was one of the leaders in the Chap-Ieau strike. He is not a red; he was bom in Canada. I should like to read one paragraph in which he makes allusion to himself, as follows:
Personally I am a Canadian citizen of British pioneer stock, born, reared and schooled in Bromley township, Renfrew county till January 1. 1927, when I came to the unorganized districts in the vicinity of Chapleau, where I have made my living since as bushman, track worker, sawmill hand, river driver, trapper and prospector. At present I am a property holder in Sudbury district as holding a number of mining claims in the Swayze gold area near here.
This man claims he has nothing to do with radicalism or communism. It is always easy to attempt to throw a smoke-screen around strike activities and give them a bad name, but the fact remains that some of these men are suffering. They realize that the government can remedy the situation. The legislation passed only a few days ago in the province of Quebec will help to remedy the injustices which have existed in that province. I can speak as a labouring man and as an axeman, and I really believe the situation to-day is not much better than it was twenty years ago. What applies to the province of Quebec applies just as forcibly to the province of Ontario.
Last fall I visited some of these lumbering camps. I found some of them to be all right but others were not. In certain camps a human being should not be allowed to live much less to sleep. There seemed to be no attempt at cleanliness, in fact, filthiness seemed to reign supreme. These camps I refer to are not even in my riding but I make a sincere appeal on behalf of the men. The strikes which occurred in my own riding

were settled and I would not like to see a repetition of what happened there. Hon. members in this parliament or members of the provincial legislature should not be willing to see such conditions exist in Canada; they are not worthy of our great country and our great natural resources, and they certainly are not worthy of our provincial and federal governments. I know the minister understands the language I am speaking and I think he wants to improve the situation. As he said a few moments ago, he took the initiative in settling the strikes which occurred in our own section, but conditions are still unsettled around Chapleau. Regardless of what some may say, that strike is not settled. A number of strikers have been kept on direct relief for the last five, six or seven weeks by the provincial and federal governments. These men are Canadians, both natural born and naturalized, and they deserve as much consideration as any other citizens.
I make this appeal to the minister because I know it is within the powers of the government to remedy the present situation. The citizens of Canada should realize the situation which exists in these lumbering camps. I listened to the two previous speakers and I think they realize just as I do that this government should have power to relieve the situation. These lumbermen are worthy citizens; they have helped and will keep on helping to build up the prosperity of Canada.

Under item 165 I asked the minister whether any boards had been established, and I think he said that that matter would come under item 168. I understand that this vote is used largely to get the employer and employee together to investigate, discuss, confer and bring about satisfactory labour conditions. In view of the conditions which existed throughout Canada last year, how does the minister explain the decrease in this vote? How could there be a decrease if the amount of conciliation work which ought to have been done was not done?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
In my estimation these conciliation officers did very fine work last year. While there were some unfortunate strikes, comparatively speaking they were very few. The conciliation officer now does the work which the conciliation boards were set up to do years ago. There have been no new boards set up, nor have any of the old ones functioned for many years. The conciliation officer tries to settle disputes by conciliation thereby doing away with the necessity of

Supply-Labour-Conciliation Act
setting up boards under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. If a strike can be settled or a dispute smoothed out, there is no necessity of going further.
The adjustment is done by an individual rather than a board?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

I realize the difficulty a federal minister of labour would have in connection with a complaint such as that made by the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette). Our federal laws hardly cover such a matter, inasmuch as the natural resources come within the jurisdiction of the Drovinees. Our Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is not framed to deal with matters of the kind. The great difficulty which I believe the minister finds in northern Ontario, as I found when I had the honour of being minister of labour, is the lack of cooperation by the provincial governments, and especially by the Minister of Lands and Forests and the Minister of Labour of the province of Ontario. The Minister of Labour for Ontario had full authority. He had at his command the provincial laws with which to deal with troubles in the lumber camps in northern Ontario; and when the outbreak started, instead of sending in someone to investigate, what did he do? He sent the provincial police in to find out whether any of the lumber workers were violating the laws of the province or of the dominion. I remember well that when one of his own fellow party men, the mayor of Fort William, wired the Minister of Lands and Forests that he ought to make an investigation because the lumber operators claimed that it was the lumbermen and the radicals who were causing the strike-lie claimed that the radicals were blaming the lumber operators-his reply to the mayor of Fort William was, "We have already had the matter investigated by the provincial police and we have not found up to the present time anyone violating the law." In other words, a minister of the provincial government, with the authority of the law at his command, started to treat Canadians the way I am sure people would not be treated in chat much discussed country, Russia. We find a labour dispute in Ontario, the banner province of this dominion, and a minister of the government of that province sends a wire to the mayor of Fort William, "We have already had the matter investigated by the provincial police and we have not yet found anyone violating the law." That is the method by which the Minister of Lands and
Forests undertakes to investigate labour disputes in Ontario, and I can well understand the federal Minister of Labour being handicapped by reason of the fact that he had no authority. And that is evidence that he had no cooperation from the province. I had to make a speech in order to bring to the attention of the Minister of Lands and Forests the fact that he had authority but had not exercised it-authority embodied in legislation passed unanimously by the legislature in 1924, after being amended by the Hon. Mr. Ferguson, then premier. He had that authority to deal with labour disputes in any industries that were using the natural resources. He had the right to investigate whether the men were receiving living wages or not. He had the right to find out whether the operators were paying these living wages, and he had the right to adjust the price of timber, the raw material in the bush, so as to permit these men to obtain a living wage. I wrote him once myself, calling his attention to the fact that he had this authority, and I pointed out to him that there was this resolution. What do you think his answer was? I want to direct the attention of the next premier of Ontario to his answer. He said, "I understood that this was a pious resolution passed by the Ontario legislature." In other words, he was going to take no notice of a resolution passed by the Ontario legislature; he thought it was a pious resolution that meant nothing. Anyhow, he acted upon it, because when the newspaper men went to him and asked him about it he said, "We are still considering it"-that is to say, they were still considering, in 1933,. taking action on a resolution passed unanimously by the legislature in 1924. Finally he called in the lumber operators and reduced their dues from $1.80 to $1 a cord. Now,-the complaint made by my hon. friend from Timiskaming is this-I have just read his letter-that when Chapleau's timber was reduced from $1.80 to $1 a cord the operator got the full value of the $1.80 and not the men referred to by the hon. gentleman.
That is the sort of treatment we get in northern Ontario, and when anyone complains of injustice the cry goes up, "Radicalism, communism, reds", and a few men are sent to penitentiary and made martyrs. That is what is taking place in northern Ontario. I am not going to refer to the strike in Stratford.
I know the Minister of Labour had nothing to do with it:	I hope at least he had not. I
hope he was not responsible for sending a regiment of soldiers with tanks and machine guns to subdue a few girls on strike in Strat-
1418	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Conciliation Act
ford. But the Ontario government ordered out troops, who went there with machine guns and tanks and paraded up and down the streets. That is the way they practise conciliation in Ontario. I do not think they shot any of these girls. The girls were on strike there because they were being paid two cents a chicken for plucking chickens, and one can imagine young Canadian women being compelled to strike in order to get one cent more per chicken. But when they sought to get a reasonable wage the Ontario government ordered out the troops, respectable troops, men who should command the respect of the people; they were ordered out with their tanks and rifles and machine guns.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
But they did it at the
request of the mayor of the town, did they not?

It matters not who requested it. If they had made the request of the Minister of Labour would he have ordered out machine guns to meet these girls just because the mayor or an alderman or one of the ministers of the Ontario government had requested it? The Ontario government were responsible for it, and they will be held responsible. I hope the federal Minister of Labour had nothing to do with it, because he is responsible for enough now. But that is the method adopted in Ontario. I can recall when there was a strike in Kapuskasing in the Spruce Falls Pulp and Paper Company. It happened during my term of office. The men were dismissed because they belonged to a union. On a Sunday afternoon the heads of the union were elected, president, secretary, Secretary-treasurer and so on, and at night, about midnight, the foreman went round and touched them in bed and gave them their time check and told them to get out because they belonged to a union. It was Sir Robert Borden who signed the treaty of Versailles which contained section 13 giving the right of freedom of association in this country; yet the present Minister of Mines and Forests, Mr. Finlayson, in the then Ferguson government of Ontario, allowed men to be dismissed who were doing work in connection with the natural resources of that province. I telegraphed the then premier of Ontario, the same as the present Minister of Labour might do, to ask for cooperation from the provincial government. I told him of the situation after I had investigated and ascertained that the men were in the right, found out the truth. What does the committee think was the reply I received? It was that as long as the company was carrying out its agreement with the

crown, they had no desire to interfere with its internal affairs. In other words, as long as the company paid the province of Ontario so much for stumpage and so much per horse power for the water it was using, they did not care whether it sacrificed the men, or whether it violated the treaty of Versailles and its provisions or anything else; they had no concern whatever in the matter. The situation was the same this year in northern Ontario- a government sitting in Toronto without any conception of decency for the working men and the working women and girls of the province either in Stratford or in the northern section. I have an affidavit from two men, a young Frenchman and a Scotchman who were sent from Winnipeg to the 'head of the lakes.
Were they communists?

No, they were just as good citizens as any who are sitting in the house at the present time. There is always somebody over there who wants to get on Hansard and who is afraid to stand up and let us know who he is.

I asked that question
and I am not afraid to stand up and ask it.

All right; the hon. gentleman is a manly fellow. These two young men were sent down to work with a lumber company at the head of the lakes. They were teamsters and they worked by the day for twenty-eight days. They were awakened between three and four o'clock in the morning to get their teams ready to go out for a load before breakfast. Then they had to go into the bush for a load after supper. They had to put their teams up at night and it was ten o'clock at night before they got through with their work. At the end of twenty-eight days one had $1 coming to him and the other had $1.15. Their railroad fare and the few things they had purchased in the camp had been deducted out of their pay. The result was that they were left stranded at the head of the lakes about $7.50 short of paying their fare home to Winnipeg. I suppose if they had started to sing the Internationale they would have been arrested as communists. What would you expect of men who had been treated like that in this banner province of Ontario, as our friends opposite so glibly call it? I sympathize with the federal Minister of Labour when he has to be questioned on the floor of the house about the settlement of strikes in northern Ontario or any other section under the jurisdiction of the Ontario government, because I am satisfied,

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
nowithstanding what he may say in regard to the matter, neither was he solicitous of getting nor would he get any cooperation from the present provincial government even if he had solicited it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Administration, Employment Offices Coordination Act, $8,000.
What is the reason for the reduction in this vote, and by how much has it been reduced since the present government came into power?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: This vote has been pretty well discussed on the two previous items. It covers merely the administration of the offices under the Employment Offices Coordination Act and deals with travelling expenses, telephone, telegraph, printing and stationery, repairs to equipment and sundries. The total amount spent last year to December 31, 1933, was just S3,228.49, so there is really no necessity for voting more money than one has to spend. Of course, if I wanted to spend money I think I could go ahead and do it, but when it is not necessary I do not feel like doing it.

I asked that question
because if it is the intention of the present government to introduce a scheme of unemployment insurance, it will be necessary that they avail themselves of these employment offices; that is, if they are going to follow the policy adopted by the British government in that regard. Perhaps this might be the time to ask the minister how far the government has gone in the formulation of a policy in connection with unemployment insurance. I would ask the minister that question now.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It will be noted that this
vote does not interfere with the one which follows later on, the one which is authorized by the revised statutes of 1927, chapter 57,
S150,000,	and refers only to the items which I have mentioned.
With respect to unemployment insurance, I am not prepared to-night to outline any course which the government may take. The subject is a very large and baffling one and anyone who hurries into it without being fully equipped with the information and the consequences that might follow from failure, would not be adopting the course of wisdom.

From the remarks of the minister am I to understand that it is not the intention of the government at any time during this session to bring before the house a policy in connection with unemployment insurance. I am not unmindful of the acute
problems arising out of the adoption of such legislation in this country, or of the declarations made by responsible ministers of the present government in connection with such a scheme. But I think the house and the country, in view of those declarations, have a right to know whether it is the intention of the government this session to make a concrete announcement of policy in regard to the introduction of a scheme of unemployment insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No one knows better than does the hon. member that in matters of government policy such as the one to which he has referred I should not be called upon to indicate nor shall I indicate what course the government may take when it sees fit to adopt one. At the present time I am not in a position to indicate to the members of the committee what course the government may take.

I say very frankly that
I think that in the course of a depression such as that through which we have been passing, the Department of Labour should be the outstanding department of the government.

The hon.
member's question is out of order.
Why?

It may be awkward,
but I think it is not out of order.

It is
irrelevant to the subject matter now under debate, which is the question of "Administration, Employment Offices Coordination Act."

I would point out,
from some knowledge of the procedure in the adoption of unemployment insurance in other countries, that if you look to the British precedent, which this country has largely followed, you will find that unemployment insurance has been largely built up around the establishment of what are known there as employment exchanges, which correspond to the employment offices we have in this country. Under this vote I took the opportunity, which I think is my prerogative, of asking the question I did, in view of the reduction in expenditure in connection with these exchanges, and having in mind that possibly the government were economizing in a direction contrary to the declaration of federal ministers in connection with the adoption of an unemployment insurance scheme. Arising out of that I think it is a perfectly fair
1420	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
observation for me to make at this time that insufficient attention has been paid to the Department of Labour by this government in view of the present depression. I think that department is one of the most important under the jurisdiction of the federal government. I say this in a kindly way; I think the present minister is overburdened. The functions of the Department of Immigration are enough in themselves to occupy fully the time of one minister, in view of the many decisions he has to make in connection with the work of that department. We are confronted, I understand, with an enormous building program in this country, and we have the oft repeated promises that the government are going to bring down an unemployment insurance measure. I think under this vote we have a right to question the intentions of the government in that regard. It would be different if the government in its judgment had led the people to believe that they were opposed to the principle of unemployment insurance.

The hon.
member is out of order on that point. The question of the advisability of the government's bringing in an unemployment insurance measure is set down for discussion under public bills and orders, and has been already the subject of a debate which is not yet concluded. Further, in my opinion the hon. member has no right to ask the Minister of Labour what the government's policy is.

I take
issue with you, Mr. Chairman. Under the estimates we are entitled to ask the administration any question about any matter of government policy whatever. I submit that the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) is quite within his rights.

Not in
asking as to the future policy of the government.

I beg
pardon; this is the only opportunity we have, under the estimates. When we are spending public money it is the well known right of parliament to ask any responsible minister about any feature of government policy. The hon. member for East Hamilton has demonstrated that these employment offices may well come into a scheme of unemployment insurance. I certainly resent any restriction of the discussion.

First may I remind the hon. member that he has no right to lecture the chair.
IMr. Mitchell.]
May I say with all due deference that the chair has no right to lecture me.

In the
second place, while hon. members have the right to discuss the actions or the past policy of the government, in my opinion they have no right in committee to ask a minister to forecast the future proposals of the government in regard to any particular matter of policy.
Where is the rule?
It is not raised in the matter before the committee, and it is out of order under the rule which says that where a matter is under debate in the house it cannot be discussed here.
May I ask you to quote the rule?
The rule is that the Prime Minister answers for them all.
His master's voice.
Surely if the matter is before the house and not disposed of we may discuss it here?
The subject of unemployment insurance is not before the committee.
It has not been disposed of, and as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) points out, it is the prerogative of this committee to discuss any matter of public policy.
May I ask you to quote the rule?
I am geb-ting it.

It is
about time you got it, I think.
Send for the Prime Minister.

Standing order 41, paragraph 293, section (d) reads:
Besides the prohibitions contained in this standing order, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking, must not:
(a) anticipate discussion on a motion set down for future consideration;
Which is the motion that is on the order paper-

We agree with you, but that is not the point.

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
-and the debate on which has not yet been concluded.
May I suggest, then, that the item be allowed to stand, if we cannot discuss the subject because there is something already on the order paper.
Which will never come up again this session.
Surely before voting money we have the right to discuss the question.
May I point out that the discussion in regard to unemployment insurance is not likely to come up again this session, because next Wednesday is likely to be the last private members' day.

Hon. members cannot get away from the rule by an anticipation of what in their judgment may or may not happen on account of the state of the order paper. Once a matter is down on the order paper for discussion and the discussion has not been concluded, it is not proper for an hon. member to say that because it is in a certain position on the order paper it is not likely to come up.
There is another reason why I think the matter is out of order, namely that unemployment insurance, while it may be a side issue of the particular vote now before the committee, is not really relevant to the vote.

That is for us to find out, I think. The vote in question is " Administration, Employment Offices Coordination Act." A question was raised by the hon. member for East Hamilton, who asked the Minister of Labour if it was the intention of himself and the administration to bring in a plan of unemployment insurance this year which might involve expenditure under this item. I suggest that this committee is entitled in all fairness to ask any question of a responsible minister in regard to any matter that arises as a result of the vote under discussion. I suggest that the question of the hon. member is quite in order.
I have already ruled.
Then I am appealing from your ruling.
That is a different matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the chairman's ruling is absolutely right, on the ground first
that the question of unemployment insurance is already on the order paper. I recall that a preceding government, when Mr. Speaker Lemieux was in the chair, kept a question on the order paper for months for the purpose of preventing discussion. It was held that we could not discuss it, on account of the rule under which hon. members may not anticipate in any discussion a matter that appears on the order paper. That rule should be maintained. I see no objection to the question asked by the hon. member for East Hamilton; that is one thing. But I see a great deal of objection to the discussion upon which he is entering on the subject of unemployment insurance. Let him ask his question and the minister will answer it.
He did ask it, and the minister did not answer it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But he is not content with that; he has entered on an elaborate discussion of the whole problem of unemployment insurance. I submit he is not entitled to do that.

I would like to point out, as I was the author of the resolution that is being talked about, that it has a different bearing from that now given to it by the hon. Minister of Justice and by you, sir. The motion I proposed reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the most effective way to ensure protection during periods of unemployment, which unemployment insurance should provide, is to make such legislation national in its scope.
That does not necessarily involve the policy of the government with regard to unemployment insurance; I may have spoken of that, but perhaps I was out of order. The actual fact recorded in the resolution is that such protection should be national in its scope, and we might have agreed on that without getting very much closer to the policy of the government with regard to unemployment insurance. There is a distinction here. As long as the hon. member keeps away from the question whether or not unemployment insurance should be national in its scope, it does not appear to me that he would come within the terms of this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

speechtext: I can easily see where the question is quite relevant to the vote now before the house. This item is for the administration of the Employment Offices Coordination Act, and it shows a reduction of $4,000. The hon. member for East Hamilton asks, and I think rightly, if it is not a fact that if there is going to be such a thing as an unemployment insurance scheme this vote would require to be enlarged. That is where the relevancy comes in, and I think the question is quite proper.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I must take issue with
the hon. member. The vote that possibly might be affected would be that under the revised statutes of 1927, chapter 57, organization and coordination of employment offices. That might have to be enlarged, but I cannot link this item up with the question of unemployment insurance.

I do not know whether I am out of order, of course, but if the minister has made any study of unemployment insurance he must know that the scheme in Great Britain was built around the employment exchanges in that country. The first thing you must have in a scheme of unemployment insurance is the development of labour exchanges from one end of this dominion to the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is not the item
inder consideration.

The Prime Minister
says that is not the item, but this item provides for the administration of these employment offices. I wondered whether the government had given up the idea, for this session at least, of introducing a scheme of unemployment insurance, and I merely asked the question because I think the country has a right to know, in view of the recent conference in connection with this matter, whether it is the intention of the government to go forward with a policy of this kind during the present session of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I thought I answered that question a while ago, when I told the hon.

member that the policy of the government with respect to unemployment insurance would be made known when that policy was decided upon, but that policy has not been decided upon by the government as yet.

When is it going to be
decided upon?

I think the hon. member would have been quite in order had he asked the minister whether this item contained any provision for unemployment insurance, and he would have been answered in the negative, as he has been answered. I think he was out of order, when he got beyond that and asked the minister to forecast the future legislative program of the government with regard to unemployment insurance.
You are merely assuming what is in the back of your mind.
When the minister says no, is there no opportunity for us to discuss the possibility of unemployment insurance?
Not under this vote.

Then may I direct your attention to the statement made by the minister that the vote which might be affected was authorized under chapter 57 of the revised statutes, 1927. This is authorized by statute, so are we to take it that we must amend the statute in order to consider this question? How are we going to do it?

The question could be considered by the house in a number of ways, but it cannot be considered under this vote when the minister has stated that the government has not decided on its program with regard to unemployment insurance, and that this vote does not contain any provision for it.
Then may I ask to what extent the government has set the machinery in motion with the idea of bringing in a system of unemployment insurance?

Have we to take your
word that the government has no policy regarding unemployment insurance? You just made the statement.
The minister has already given his answer.

I do not think that is
true; you just made the statement as chairman of this committee.

Wheat Agreement-Mr. Bennett

I would
ask the hon. member to take his seat. The minister has made his statement on that point.

We are
not satisfied with the statement.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
